analysis.one_liner: Ends the TARP bank bailout program and directs repayments to pay down the national debt.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in December 2009 and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut down the Treasury's authority to hand out new Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) bailout money, sent every TARP repayment, dividend, and profit into a Treasury account used to pay down the national debt, and required every bank still holding TARP funds to publish a report every six months explaining how it was using that money.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, because bailout repayments and any profits would be locked in for debt paydown rather than available for new spending, and the public, because banks holding TARP money would have to disclose publicly how they used it. New bailout authority would end, so no future federal money could flow to banks under this program.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the Treasury Secretary's authority under sections 101 and 102 of the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act upon enactment, ending new TARP assistance.
Requires all TARP repayments, dividends, profits, and other funds received on or after enactment to be deposited in a Treasury account and used to pay down the national debt.

Requires every financial institution that received TARP assistance to report every six months, while any assistance is outstanding, on how it is using the money, with the reports made public including on the institution's website.

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions receiving TARP funds, which would lose the possibility of further federal assistance under the program and would face new public reporting duties on how they used taxpayer money. Consumers and credit markets could also bear some cost if abruptly cutting off bailout authority unsettled a financial system still recovering from the 2008 crisis.

drawbacks.text: Terminating the Treasury's TARP assistance authority immediately upon enactment, as the bill directs, would have cut off a crisis tool in December 2009 while the financial system was still recovering, which critics of early TARP shutdowns argued could have destabilized lending and markets.

Directing all TARP repayments and profits to debt paydown is largely symbolic bookkeeping; the amounts were already flowing to the Treasury, so the bill's main practical effect was to end future assistance and add reporting, not to recover money that would otherwise have been lost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency requirement was a real, modest win for the public, and locking bailout repayments toward debt paydown narrowed how leftover program money could be used. But the core provision, instantly ending bailout authority, traded away flexibility to respond to renewed financial stress for little measurable gain, since most TARP money had already been disbursed. A phased shutdown with the reporting mandate would have captured most of the benefit with less risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Thaddeus McCotter introduced the bill on December 16, 2009, joined by Representative Spencer Bachus as its one cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No committee action, floor vote, or further step ever followed; the bill's last recorded action was the referral, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks holding TARP funds and Treasury officials retained the status quo: bailout authority stayed open and no enhanced public reporting was imposed, since the bill died without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate TARP authority, route repayments to debt paydown, and require semiannual public reporting by TARP recipients.

for.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only other member to do so.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 16, 2009 and never reported the bill, held no markup, and never advanced it to the floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both named supporters were Republicans in a Democratic-controlled House, and the Democratic-run Financial Services Committee took no action; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have ended any prospect of further bailout money under TARP and forced banks still holding assistance to publicly explain every six months how they were using it. Their interest in continued federal support and lighter disclosure ran against the taxpayers footing the bill.

The bill would have stripped the Treasury Secretary of authority to extend new TARP assistance and locked repayments toward debt paydown, removing discretion the administration was still using during the financial recovery.
